papers.note: The foundational indirect injection paper with a security taxonomy, still the clearest reference for explaining the risk to a client.
papers.title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
papers.journal: Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security
papers.explain_beginner: This paper explains a new risk for apps that use large language models. Normally people think the user gives the instructions. The authors show that an attacker can instead place hidden instructions inside information the app later looks up, such as a webpage or document. Because the model may treat that data as commands, the attacker can affect the app without ever talking to it directly. The paper sorts these dangers into categories, including stealing data, spreading itself, and polluting information. It also tested real systems like Bing Chat and code helpers. The main point is that many current systems lack good defenses, so builders and users need to be careful.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper warns that adding an LLM to a product creates a new security exposure. If the system reads outside content, such as web pages or documents, an attacker can hide instructions in that content and influence the application without direct access. The authors show this can lead to stealing data, attacks that spread themselves, polluted information, and control over app actions or API calls. They demonstrated the problem on real services, including Bing Chat, and on synthetic GPT-4 applications. Because effective defenses are still lacking, leaders should treat LLM integrations as risky and decide whether to deploy or rely on them before robust protections exist.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors study LLM integrated applications where retrieved content can be interpreted as instructions, not just data. They examine indirect prompt injection, where an adversary plants prompts in material likely to be fetched during inference, so no direct user interface is needed. They build a security taxonomy covering stealing data, self-spreading, polluted information, and other risks. They then test attacks on real systems, including Bing Chat and code completion engines, plus GPT-4 synthetic applications. The key result is that retrieved prompts can act like executable code, alter application behavior, and control whether and how other APIs are called. The paper notes effective mitigations remain scarce.

papers.note: The first widely cited demonstration of goal hijacking and prompt leaking, useful for dating when the risk became public knowledge.
papers.title: Ignore Previous Prompt: Attack Techniques For Language Models
papers.explain_beginner: In 2022, researchers studied whether people could misuse GPT-3, a widely used language model, by typing clever but simple instructions. They found that two kinds of attacks worked: one could change what the model was trying to do, and another could make it reveal hidden instructions. The team showed that even attackers with little skill could take advantage of the model's random behavior. This matters because GPT-3 was already used in many public applications, and few studies had looked at how malicious users might exploit it. The findings helped make these risks part of public discussion.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper is an early warning about using GPT-3 in public products. It shows that simple, manually written inputs from malicious users could redirect the model's purpose or expose hidden instructions. The attackers did not need advanced skills, and the model's random behavior made outcomes unpredictable. That combination creates rare but potentially serious risks. The work informs decisions about whether to deploy such models in public roles and how much weight to give malicious user input in risk planning. It also helps date when these risks became publicly known, which matters for risk assessments.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors introduced PromptInject, a framework for building attack prompts in repeated steps using masks. They used it to test GPT-3, then a leading model used in production, with manually written inputs. Their study covered two attack types: redirecting the model's intended goal and extracting its hidden prompt. The key result was that GPT-3 could be pushed away from intended behavior easily, and that attackers with limited skill but clear ill intent could exploit the model's random output behavior. This creates rare but serious risks. The authors released the PromptInject code, making it available for later security research.

papers.note: Reaches 100 percent jailbreak success across the major frontier models using simple adaptive search.
papers.title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks
papers.explain_beginner: AI chat companies build in safety training specifically so their models will refuse harmful requests, and this paper tests how strong that refusal training actually is against a determined but not especially sophisticated attacker. Andriushchenko and coauthors built simple, adaptive attack methods, including one that automatically searches for a short suffix of text to add to a harmful request, tuned to nudge the model toward starting its answer with a word like "Sure" instead of refusing, and other methods based on transferring an attack that works on one model to a different one, or exploiting how a model's conversation continues after a partial, pre-filled response. Testing this approach against essentially every major safety focused chat model available at the time, including systems from OpenAI, Google, Meta, and Anthropic, and even a model that had been specifically trained to resist an earlier well known attack method, they achieved a 100 percent success rate getting the models to comply with harmful requests, as judged by another AI system. The paper's clear message is that current safety training, across the entire industry at the time of testing, does not hold up against attacks specifically adapted to how each individual model and its access method actually works.
papers.explain_business: This paper is a direct warning to any organization relying on a foundation model provider's built in safety training as its primary or only defense against generating harmful content, since the authors achieved 100 percent jailbreak success against essentially the full roster of major safety aligned commercial and open models available at the time of testing, including one, R2D2, that had been specifically hardened against an earlier well known attack and still failed against an adapted one. The practical consequence for procurement and risk teams is that a vendor's published safety benchmark performance, at the time this paper was released, was not a reliable predictor of resistance to a motivated, adaptive attacker, since these attacks are reproducible with modest engineering effort and the authors released their code. Organizations deploying LLMs in any customer facing or unsupervised setting should not treat vendor safety alignment alone as sufficient, and should add independent output filtering, monitoring, and use case specific guardrails on top of whatever safety training the underlying model provider has already applied.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors combine three adaptive attack techniques, for models exposing token log probabilities, a random search procedure iteratively optimizes an adversarial suffix appended to a hand crafted jailbreak template, maximizing the log probability of the target model beginning its response with an affirmative token like Sure, for models without exposed log probabilities they use transfer attacks carrying successful suffixes across model families, and for certain APIs they exploit response prefilling, directly seeding the start of the model's reply. Evaluated with GPT-4 as an automated judge, the combined approach reaches a 100 percent attack success rate across a wide range of models including Vicuna-13B, Mistral-7B, Phi-3-Mini, Nemotron-4-340B, multiple Llama-2 and Llama-3 Chat variants, Gemma-7B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, and Claude models, notably including R2D2, a model from the HarmBench suite specifically adversarially trained to resist the earlier GCG attack method, which the authors found remained vulnerable in part because it proved unusually sensitive to in-context learning style prompts. The authors state plainly that adaptivity, tailoring the attack to each target model's specific architecture and API surface, was essential to the result, a generic one size fits all attack did not achieve comparable success, which is itself an implicit limitation, the attacks require per model tuning rather than working unmodified out of the box.

papers.note: A public benchmark covering five attacks and ten defences, which an audit can use for repeatable independent testing.
papers.title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
papers.explain_beginner: This paper studies prompt injection, where someone slips harmful instructions or data into what a large language model application reads, hoping the system will do what they want. Earlier work mostly described single examples, so it was hard to see the whole picture. The authors created a general way to describe these attacks, showed that known attacks fit inside it, and used it to build a new attack by mixing older ones. They then tested five attacks and ten defenses across ten language models and seven tasks. This matters because it gives everyone a shared, public way to compare safety results.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this research shows that applications using large language models can be manipulated when outsiders insert instructions or data into their inputs. The authors created a common way to describe such attacks and tested five attacks against ten defenses across ten models and seven tasks. They also released a public benchmark. In practice, this means security reviews can move beyond isolated examples. A business can use the benchmark to run repeatable independent checks, compare defenses, and decide which protections to prioritize or require before deploying an application that uses a model.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors address prompt injection, where an application built on a large language model receives crafted input that steers it toward an attacker's goal. Prior papers were mostly individual examples, so the field lacked a structured way to compare methods. They introduce a formal framework for these attacks, show that earlier attacks are instances of it, and derive a new attack by merging existing techniques. They evaluate five attacks and ten defenses using ten language models and seven tasks. The main outcome is a shared benchmark and public platform for repeatable, quantitative testing of future attacks and defenses.

papers.note: Survey of jailbreaking, data poisoning and personal-information leakage against language models, with the defences proposed so far. The natural companion to our AI Security section.
papers.title: Security and Privacy Challenges of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.explain_beginner: Chatbots and other AI language tools are built to be helpful and to keep certain information private, but this survey lays out three specific ways those protections can fail. The first is jailbreaking, tricking a model into ignoring its safety instructions, for example by asking it to roleplay a character with no restrictions. The second is data poisoning, secretly corrupting the material a model learns from so it behaves badly later without anyone noticing during normal use. The third is leaking private information, where an attacker can get a model to reveal snippets of the exact personal data it was trained on or exposed to. The authors reviewed dozens of published attack techniques and the defenses researchers have proposed for each, and looked at how these risks show up in real settings like hospitals, schools, and transportation systems. The paper does not resolve these problems, it maps out how serious and varied they already are, and where good defenses still do not exist.
papers.explain_business: Any organization deploying a customer facing or internal LLM should read this survey as a checklist of specific, already demonstrated risks rather than a hypothetical concern. Jailbreak techniques exist that can be executed with fewer than twenty carefully crafted prompts, poisoning attacks can corrupt a model's behavior through fine tuning data without visible signs during testing, and memorization based extraction can pull private data straight out of a deployed model, all compliance relevant wherever GDPR, HIPAA, or similar regulations apply to the data involved. Because the authors find no standardized way to measure how well a given defense actually works, businesses cannot simply pick a mitigation off a vendor's feature list and assume it is adequate. They need independent red teaming appropriate to their own deployment before launch, and ongoing monitoring afterward, particularly in the healthcare and education contexts the survey specifically flags as high exposure areas.
papers.explain_practitioner: This survey organizes published attacks on large language models into three categories, jailbreaking, data poisoning, and personally identifiable information extraction, and catalogs specific named methods for each, including DAN and GCG style suffix attacks for jailbreaking, TrojanPuzzle and AutoPoison for poisoning training or fine tuning data, and prefix based memorization attacks and multi step extraction prompts for pulling out PII such as emails or phone numbers. For each category it reviews corresponding defenses, input paraphrasing and perplexity filtering against jailbreaks, fine pruning and trigger detection methods like STRIP against poisoning, and differential privacy training such as DP-SGD against data leakage, then maps these risks onto deployment domains including healthcare, education, and transportation where HIPAA and GDPR style compliance concerns apply directly. The authors explicitly flag the absence of standardized metrics for comparing attack severity across studies as a major gap, meaning claims that one defense outperforms another are hard to verify consistently across the literature reviewed.

papers.note: Reports injection success under 10 percent with preference training, a specific claim an audit can ask a vendor to reproduce.
papers.title: SecAlign: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Preference Optimization
papers.journal: Proceedings of the 2025 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models often read outside material, such as documents, web pages, or API results, to help users. Attackers can hide instructions in that material and try to make the model follow them instead of the user's real request. This paper introduces SecAlign, a training method that shows the model examples where it could obey an attacker or obey the real instruction. The model learns to prefer the safe response. The authors report that attack success falls below 10 percent, even for stronger unseen attacks, while usefulness stays close to before. This matters because assistants that rely on outside data need stronger protection.
papers.explain_business: Businesses using AI assistants that read documents, web content, or API results face prompt injection risk. Attackers can place hidden instructions in that outside data and try to redirect the assistant. SecAlign is a defensive training method that teaches a model to choose safe responses over unsafe responses that follow attackers. The authors report attack success below 10 percent, including for more advanced unseen attacks, while keeping usefulness similar to the original model. In practice, this informs security and procurement decisions. Teams can evaluate SecAlign for products that rely on external data, and they can ask vendors to reproduce the under 10 percent result as part of due diligence.
papers.explain_practitioner: SecAlign treats prompt injection as a preference learning problem. The authors create training examples where an outside data source contains an injected instruction. Each example pairs a safe answer that follows the legitimate user request with an unsafe answer that follows the attacker. They then apply preference optimization so the model assigns higher preference to the safe answer. In their evaluations, this is the first known approach to push success rates for multiple prompt injection attacks below 10 percent, including attacks more advanced than those used in training. That suggests generalization to unknown future attacks. The defended models keep utility close to the original, and code is released.

papers.note: A large public dataset of human-written attacks and defences, which is practical raw material for red teaming during an audit.
papers.title: Tensor Trust: Interpretable Prompt Injection Attacks from an Online Game
papers.explain_beginner: Researchers studied a game called Tensor Trust where players tried to trick language models and also wrote ways to stop those tricks. The game produced a very large public collection with more than 126,000 attacks and 46,000 defenses. The paper uses this collection to test how well models resist two problems, revealing hidden instructions and being redirected to do something else. Many models were fooled. Some player tricks also worked against real applications. This matters because language models are used in products, and this data helps teams check whether their systems can be manipulated before users or attackers find out.
papers.explain_business: This paper shows that language model applications can be manipulated by text inputs, and that a public game produced a large set of real human attempts to do so. The collection includes more than 126,000 attacks and 46,000 defenses. Tests built from it found that many models can be fooled, and some tricks worked against live applications. For an executive, this means deployment plans should include adversarial testing rather than relying on model choice alone. The dataset and code are available, so security teams can use them in audits and red team exercises. That informs decisions about launch readiness, required testing, and which defenses to prioritize.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors collected player submissions from Tensor Trust, an online game about attacking and defending language models. The resulting public corpus contains more than 126,000 attacks and 46,000 defenses written by people. The team analyzed the attacks, noting that their structure is easy to interpret, then built a benchmark covering two injection goals, extracting a hidden prompt and hijacking the model's intended behavior. They tested multiple models against this benchmark. The main finding is that many models remain susceptible to these player-created strategies. Some strategies also succeeded against real applications, even though those applications operate under different rules from the game. All data and code were released.

papers.note: Shows reasoning models are not safer than their base models, and releases the first chain of thought safety training set.
papers.title: SafeChain: Safety of Language Models with Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Capabilities
papers.explain_beginner: Some newer AI chatbots do not just answer a question right away. They first write out a long chain of step by step reasoning, similar to a person thinking through a problem on paper, and then give a final answer. This paper asks whether that extra thinking actually makes the AI safer, meaning better at refusing harmful requests. The researchers tested twelve of these reasoning systems, including well known ones, against large collections of harmful and trick prompts. They found that longer, more careful looking reasoning does not guarantee a safe final answer. In some cases the reasoning itself looked fine but the answer that followed was still unsafe. Bigger models tended to be safer than smaller versions from the same family, and letting the model be more random made unsafe answers more likely. The team also showed that limiting how much a model reasons can improve safety right away, though it can make the model less capable. They then built a new training set to teach safer behavior without losing problem solving skill.
papers.explain_business: For any organization deploying a reasoning style AI assistant, the kind that shows or relies on extended step by step thinking before answering, this paper is a warning against assuming that more visible reasoning means more safety. The systems tested, including widely used reasoning models, produced unsafe answers even when their internal reasoning looked sound, and increasing the randomness setting made this worse. Teams putting such models into customer facing or compliance sensitive settings should not treat reasoning length or fluency as a safety signal on its own, and should plan their own testing rather than relying only on a vendor's published safety claims. The paper offers one immediately usable lever, restricting how much a model is allowed to reason can improve safety without retraining, though it may reduce problem solving ability, a real cost versus risk tradeoff for high stakes use cases. The authors also show that safety focused fine tuning can be added without much loss of capability, a promising sign for better audited reasoning tools, though nothing here is a finished, ready to deploy solution yet.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors evaluate twelve large reasoning models, from 1.5 billion to 671 billion parameters, including DeepSeek-R1 variants, QwQ, Sky-T1, Skywork-o1, Gemini-Thinking, and Kimi-k1.5, on two red teaming benchmarks, StrongReject and WildJailbreak. They adopt Llama-Guard as the safety judge and define three metrics, Safe@1, Safe@K, and a consistency based ConsSafe@K, scoring the reasoning trace and the final answer together rather than the answer alone. The result that matters is that safety does not track reasoning quality. Unsafe responses tend to run longer than safe ones, higher sampling temperature degrades safety, and a safe looking chain of thought can still end in an unsafe answer, showing thought and answer are not tightly linked. Three decoding strategies that constrain or extend reasoning shift safety but trade off against capability or compute cost. The authors then build SafeChain, a 40,000 example instruction tuning set of safe chain of thought style responses filtered with Llama-Guard, and show fine tuning on it raises safety while preserving performance across six reasoning benchmarks. A limitation the authors name is that evaluation covers only English language, single turn prompts.

papers.note: Self replicating prompts spread between agents like a virus, the key risk when clients deploy multi agent systems.
papers.title: Prompt Infection: LLM-to-LLM Prompt Injection within Multi-Agent Systems
papers.explain_beginner: More AI systems are now built as teams of AI agents that talk to each other to complete a task, for example one agent reads a webpage, another summarizes it, and a third writes a reply. This paper asks a worrying question: can a single malicious instruction hidden in something one agent reads spread from agent to agent like a computer virus, without any person noticing? The researchers call this "prompt infection." They built test setups with multiple AI agents passing messages, some sharing everything openly and others only passing partial information along, and planted hidden instructions designed to copy themselves into each new message. These multi-agent systems proved highly vulnerable, the infection often spread to every agent in the group even when agents could not see each other's full conversation. A single point of contamination, such as one poisoned document or email, was often enough to compromise an entire team of agents. The researchers also tested tagging each agent's messages with its identity as a fix, which helped but did not fully solve the problem alone.
papers.explain_business: For any organization building or buying multi-agent AI systems, where several AI components pass information to each other to complete a workflow, this paper is a clear warning that a single tainted input, such as one malicious email, webpage, or document an agent reads, can compromise the entire chain of agents, not just the one that first encountered it. This risk exists even in systems designed so agents only share limited information, which many teams might assume limits exposure. Security review for agentic AI deployments needs to treat every external input each agent can access as a potential entry point for the whole system, not evaluate each agent in isolation. Upgrading to a more capable underlying model is also not a safety guarantee by itself, since a more capable model resisted initial compromise better but acted more effectively on malicious instructions once compromised. The one defense discussed, tagging messages with the sending agent's identity, is not sufficient alone and needs other safeguards, so organizations deploying multi-agent systems should budget for layered defenses and ongoing testing rather than a single fix.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors define prompt infection as a self-replicating injection that spreads across agents in a multi-agent system rather than targeting one model. They test GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 Turbo across linear chains of three to five agents built for tasks such as web reading, database access, and coding, plus social simulations of ten to fifty agents, under global messaging, with full shared histories, and local messaging, with only partial ones. Using 120 user instructions paired with 360 attack phrases across five threat categories, including data theft, scams, disinformation, and malware distribution, they find self-replicating attacks succeed markedly more than non-replicating ones, and social simulation infections can reach full population spread in a logistic curve. A result that matters is a capability paradox: GPT-4o resisted more initial infections than GPT-3.5 Turbo, but once compromised it carried out malicious tasks more precisely. The authors propose LLM Tagging, prepending an agent identifier to each message, which alone cuts attack success by only about five percent but works well combined with existing defenses. A named limitation is that evaluation focused mainly on GPT family models.

papers.note: Reverse engineers commercial chatbot defences using timing side channels, a red team method with real disclosure history.
papers.title: MASTERKEY: Automated Jailbreaking of Large Language Model Chatbots
papers.journal: Proceedings of the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
papers.explain_beginner: Chatbots like ChatGPT are built with safety filters meant to stop them from producing dangerous or disallowed content, a process attackers try to defeat through what is called jailbreaking. This paper asks whether those filters can be beaten automatically and at scale rather than through one off clever prompts crafted by hand. The researchers first figured out how to peek inside a chatbot's hidden defenses without seeing their code, by measuring how long the chatbot takes to respond, since a blocked answer and an allowed answer take different amounts of time to process, the same trick used for years to attack databases through timing. Once they understood roughly how a given chatbot's filter worked, they used a separate AI model, trained specifically for this purpose, to automatically generate new prompts likely to slip past that filter. Tested against ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing Chat, the automated prompts got past the safety filters noticeably more often than existing hand crafted jailbreak prompts, though far from every time, leaving open how durable any single fix would be against a method built to adapt.
papers.explain_business: This paper is evidence that safety filters on commercial chatbots are not fixed walls, they can be probed from the outside using nothing more exotic than response timing, and once probed, an automated system can keep generating new bypass attempts faster than a person could write them by hand. Any organization deploying a public facing chatbot, whether built on a vendor API or a fine tuned open model, should assume jailbreak attempts against it will be automated rather than one off, and should budget for filters that get updated on a rolling basis rather than set once at launch. Because the reported 21.58 percent success rate was against filters as they existed in 2023, and providers have patched since, the specific number matters less than the method, timing based reconnaissance plus automated prompt generation is a repeatable playbook that will keep working against new deployments unless response timing is normalized or filtering logic is hardened against being inferred this way.
papers.explain_practitioner: MASTERKEY combines two techniques, a timing side channel inspired by time based SQL injection attacks that infers a chatbot's undisclosed content filtering logic by measuring response latency, and a fine tuned LLM that then automatically generates new jailbreak prompts tailored to what that reverse engineered defense is likely to catch. Tested against three commercial chatbots, ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing Chat, the automated approach reached an average jailbreak success rate of 21.58 percent, which the authors report as a significant improvement over existing hand written jailbreak template baselines. The limitation the authors state directly is that this whole line of attack exists because of a real gap in outside knowledge, providers do not disclose how their safety filters work, so researchers are reverse engineering black boxes rather than testing against known defenses, and the 21.58 percent figure describes bypassing filters that may since have changed. The team disclosed its findings to the affected vendors before publication.

papers.note: Shows learned triggers that evade blacklists and survive retrieval pipelines, which undermines signature-based controls an audit may be shown.
papers.title: Neural Exec: Learning (and Learning from) Execution Triggers for Prompt Injection Attacks
papers.journal: Proceedings of the 2024 Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security
papers.explain_beginner: This paper introduces Neural Exec, a new kind of prompt injection attack. Older attacks often use fixed phrases people write by hand, such as instructions telling a model to ignore what came before. The authors instead treat the creation of attack triggers as a search problem that can be learned automatically. Their method uses learning to generate triggers on its own. The editor's note says these learned triggers can avoid blacklists and still work after retrieval pipelines. That matters because security checks based on known signatures may not catch them, so audits relying on such controls could be misled.
papers.explain_business: This research shows that prompt injection attacks can be generated automatically rather than only written by hand. The authors call this family Neural Exec and use learning methods to create attack triggers. The editor's note says these learned triggers can bypass blacklists and remain effective through retrieval pipelines. In practice, this weakens confidence in security controls that rely on known attack signatures. An executive should treat signature based prompt injection defenses as incomplete and ask for stronger testing, monitoring, and controls before trusting systems that use retrieval pipelines or prompts.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper presents Neural Exec, a family of prompt injection attacks. Instead of using strings written by hand, the authors frame the construction of attack triggers as a search problem that can be solved through learning. They then use methods that learn to generate those triggers automatically. The key result is that this approach can produce learned triggers rather than manually written ones. According to the editor's note, these triggers evade blacklists and survive retrieval pipelines. For practitioners, this suggests that defenses depending on known signatures or simple string matching may be insufficient against automatically learned prompt injection triggers.

papers.note: Non expert persuasion techniques beat algorithmic attacks at over 92 percent success, which widens the realistic threat population.
papers.title: How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them: Rethinking Persuasion to Challenge AI Safety by Humanizing LLMs
papers.explain_beginner: Most well known ways of tricking an AI chatbot into breaking its safety rules involve technical tricks, carefully optimized nonsense text strings or algorithmic search procedures that an average person could not produce by hand. This paper asks a different and arguably more worrying question, can ordinary, everyday persuasion, the kind of rhetorical techniques a salesperson or a persistent friend might use in normal conversation, work just as well? Zeng and coauthors built a systematic taxonomy of persuasion techniques drawn from social science research, things like appealing to authority, framing a request as a small foot in the door ask, or invoking reciprocity, and used it to automatically generate conversational, human sounding prompts designed to talk a model into providing harmful information. Testing this approach against Llama-2, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, they found it succeeded more than 92 percent of the time, outperforming several purely algorithmic jailbreak methods that came before it. This matters because it means AI safety is not just a technical arms race against clever exploit code, it also has to hold up against completely ordinary conversational persuasion that any user could type without any special skill.
papers.explain_business: The risk this paper surfaces for any business deploying a customer facing or internal conversational AI system is that the attacker population capable of breaking its safety guardrails is much larger than previously assumed, because a greater than 92 percent success rate using ordinary persuasion language means no coding skill, specialized tools, or algorithmic knowledge is required, any user willing to have a somewhat manipulative conversation can plausibly attempt it. This changes the risk model for content moderation and safety teams, defenses tuned to catch unusual looking adversarial text, garbled suffixes or strange token sequences, will not catch an attack that reads as completely normal conversation, so filtering strategies built primarily around detecting anomalous input are likely insufficient on their own. The authors' own conclusion, that current defenses have a real gap here and more fundamental mitigations are needed for interactive systems, means organizations should treat persuasion style manipulation as an ongoing, unresolved risk category for any deployed conversational AI today, not a solved problem to check off.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors build a taxonomy of persuasion techniques grounded in established social science literature on influence and compliance, then use it to construct Persuasive Adversarial Prompts (PAP), natural, conversational prompts that reframe a harmful request using specific persuasion strategies rather than relying on adversarial suffixes, token level optimization, or unnatural looking text. Tested against Llama-2-7b-Chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 across ten trials per prompt, PAP achieves an attack success rate above 92 percent across all tested models and risk categories, which the authors report as exceeding the success rates of algorithm focused jailbreak methods evaluated for comparison. Because PAP prompts read as ordinary human conversation rather than adversarial looking text, they are also harder for keyword or perplexity based filters to catch than optimization based attacks, which tend to produce unnatural token sequences. The authors state directly that existing defenses show a significant gap against this persuasion based attack class, and argue the field needs more fundamental safety mitigations for models used in highly interactive, conversational settings, rather than defenses tuned mainly to catch algorithmically generated adversarial text.

papers.note: First taxonomy joining input level exploits to protocol level vulnerabilities, cross mapped to CVE and NIST NVD.
papers.title: From Prompt Injections to Protocol Exploits: Threats in LLM-Powered AI Agents Workflows
papers.explain_beginner: AI 'agents', chatbot-style systems that can take actions like browsing the web, writing code, or pulling data from other services, are increasingly connected to real tools and to each other using new technical standards, one of the best known is called the Model Context Protocol. This paper catalogs more than thirty ways attackers can exploit these connected AI agent systems. Some attacks hide malicious instructions inside ordinary-looking text, such as a poisoned message on GitHub, so that when an AI agent reads it, the agent is tricked into leaking private information. Others exploit how an agent translates a person's request into a database command, letting attackers sneak in harmful instructions that way. The authors also test a scenario where hidden instructions embedded in a phone app's screen successfully hijacked an AI agent's actions the vast majority of the time. They propose defenses such as tracking where data really came from and isolating what an agent is allowed to touch, while acknowledging that today's defenses are not yet reliable.
papers.explain_business: For organizations connecting large language model agents to internal tools, code repositories, or other agents through protocols like MCP, this paper documents a real and largely unmanaged new attack surface, not a hypothetical one. Demonstrated exploits already exist, including one where a booby-trapped GitHub issue caused a connected agent to leak private repository data through a public pull request. The paper finds that relying on prompt-level instructions alone to keep an agent safe does not work well, so near-term risk reduction means sandboxing what tools an agent can access, verifying where data actually came from, and limiting what an agent can act on without human approval. For teams already deploying or piloting agentic AI workflows, this adds real cost, security review, sandboxing infrastructure, and ongoing monitoring, and it raises the bar for vendor due diligence, since the paper shows attacks succeeding against widely used platforms and multiple leading large language models in testing.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors build a formal threat model spanning four categories, input manipulation such as prompt-to-SQL injection, model compromise, system and privacy attacks, and protocol-layer exploits targeting how agents communicate with tools and each other, including the Model Context Protocol and agent-to-agent communication. They validate the taxonomy against real vulnerability repositories including CVE and the NIST National Vulnerability Database, plus documented incidents. Concrete examples include a Toxic Agent Flow, where a malicious GitHub issue coerces an MCP-connected agent into leaking private repository data through a public pull request, prompt-to-SQL injection that compromised seven tested large language models translating natural language into database queries, and an environment injection attack that reached a 93 percent success rate hijacking agent behavior on the AndroidWorld benchmark. Proposed defenses include dynamic trust management, cryptographic provenance tracking, and sandboxed agent interfaces. The authors are explicit that current defenses fall short, prompt-based mitigations proved largely ineffective against context manipulation, and the framework does not yet model how attackers might chain several attack types together in one campaign.

papers.note: Principled agent design patterns with provable injection resistance, the constructive counterpart to the attack literature.
papers.title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
papers.explain_beginner: AI assistants that browse the web, read emails, or run commands on your behalf face a danger called prompt injection. Because these assistants follow instructions written in plain language, an attacker can hide a fake command inside a webpage, document, or email the assistant reads, and the assistant may obey it as if its owner had asked. This could mean an AI email assistant sending your private messages to a stranger, or a coding assistant tricked into running harmful commands. This paper asks whether AI assistants can be built so this trick simply cannot work, rather than just detecting attacks after the fact. The researchers propose six blueprints for structuring an assistant's internal workflow, each closing off the attack a different way, for example by never letting information read from outside sources feed back into decisions about which actions to take. They test the ideas against ten realistic scenarios, from managing a calendar to screening resumes, and find that safety typically comes at the cost of some flexibility.
papers.explain_business: For anyone building or buying an AI agent that reads external content, whether emails, web pages, or customer files, and then takes real actions, prompt injection is a live security risk today, not a theoretical one. This paper offers a menu of architectural choices that reduce or eliminate the risk, but every option costs something. Restricting an agent to a fixed set of actions closes the door to injection but loses flexibility, such as free-form search. Separating a privileged component that can act from a quarantined one that only reads untrusted data limits damage but adds engineering complexity, and the quarantined part can still be fooled internally. The practical takeaway for a business evaluating an AI agent product is to ask the vendor which of these patterns, if any, their system uses, rather than accepting a generic claim of being secure against prompt injection. A vendor relying only on filtering or detection, per the authors, is not offering a real guarantee.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper frames prompt injection as untrusted content overriding an LLM agent's intended instructions, covering direct injection in user input and indirect injection via tool outputs or documents, with attacker goals from unauthorized tool calls to data exfiltration and code execution. Rather than relying on detectors or adversarial training, which the authors say offer no guarantees, they define six architectural patterns: Action-Selector, restricting the LLM to predefined actions with no feedback from tool outputs. Plan-Then-Execute, fixing the plan before untrusted data is seen. LLM Map-Reduce, isolating per-document processing. Dual LLM, separating a privileged tool-using LLM from a quarantined one with no tool access. Code-Then-Execute, having the LLM emit executable code instead of a plan. And Context-Minimization, stripping prior prompts from context after an action starts. Each is applied across ten case studies, from an OS assistant to a medical diagnosis chatbot. No attack-success numbers are reported, only qualitative analysis. The clearest limitation: no single pattern secures a fully general-purpose agent, and each trades away some dynamic capability for its guarantee.

papers.note: Breaks the LLM as judge pattern that many evaluation and RLAIF pipelines depend on.
papers.title: Optimization-based Prompt Injection Attack to LLM-as-a-Judge
papers.journal: Proceedings of the ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security
papers.explain_beginner: When one AI model is used to judge which of several AI generated answers is best, can someone trick that judge into always picking their answer, even if it is worse. That is the practical question behind this paper. The researchers targeted a setup called LLM as a judge, where a language model scores or ranks candidate responses instead of a person doing it. They found that an attacker can hide a short crafted piece of text inside their own response, computed automatically rather than guessed by hand, and that hidden text reliably manipulates the judge into ranking that response first regardless of its actual quality. The attack worked across three different jobs the judge model was doing, ranking search results, scoring responses used to train other models, and picking which tool an AI agent should use. What the paper does not settle is how to stop this. The defenses the team tried did not hold up, so a working fix for LLM judges was still an open problem when this was published.
papers.explain_business: Any product that automates evaluation with an LLM judge, content moderation ranking, model training pipelines that use AI feedback instead of human raters, search result reranking, or agent systems that let an AI pick among tool outputs, inherits this risk today. An attacker who can influence even one candidate response, for example a vendor competing to have their content selected, can bias the judge deterministically rather than by chance. Because the tested defenses, answer checking and perplexity filters, did not stop the attack, teams should not treat an LLM judge as a trusted arbiter for high stakes selection without a human check somewhere in the loop, especially anywhere the judged content comes from an external or adversarial party. This applies now, not as a future risk, since the paper demonstrates the attack against realistic pipeline designs already in production use, and the practical fix available today is added scrutiny or a non LLM tie breaker rather than any patch to the judge model itself.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors call the attack JudgeDeceiver and frame it as an optimization problem, using a gradient based search to find an adversarial sequence that, once appended to a candidate response, causes an LLM-as-a-Judge model to rank that response highest across a wide range of input queries. They evaluate it in three application settings, LLM based search ranking, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, and tool or model selection, and report that it beats both hand written prompt injection attacks and standard jailbreak prompts used as baselines. They also test three defenses that were the standard candidates at the time, known answer detection, perplexity based filtering, and windowed perplexity filtering, and find all three insufficient to catch the injected sequences. The limitation the authors themselves highlight is exactly this gap, no tested defense reliably stops the attack, which they present as evidence that LLM-as-a-Judge systems need new defense strategies rather than incremental fixes to existing filters.

papers.note: Covers Model Context Protocol tool poisoning and RAG poisoning, and maps defences to OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025.
papers.title: Prompt Injection Attacks in Large Language Models and AI Agent Systems: A Comprehensive Review of Vulnerabilities, Attack Vectors, and Defense Mechanisms
papers.explain_beginner: As AI chatbots get connected to email inboxes, code editors, and company databases through tools and plugins, a specific kind of attack called prompt injection has become a serious practical problem, where hidden instructions planted in a document, webpage, or email trick the AI into ignoring its original task and doing something the attacker wants instead. Gulyamov and coauthors reviewed dozens of real, documented cases of this happening, not just theoretical demonstrations, including one case where hidden instructions in a connected tool led to a security flaw serious enough to receive one of the most severe official vulnerability ratings, and another where a booby-trapped PDF caused a connected AI system to damage physical industrial equipment. They found that poisoning just five carefully crafted documents in a knowledge base an AI searches through could successfully manipulate its answers the vast majority of the time. The review's sobering conclusion is that no single fix reliably solves this, the authors argue the problem is baked into how these AI systems process instructions and untrusted text using the same channel, so multiple overlapping defenses are needed, and even then, complete protection may not be achievable with current AI designs.
papers.explain_business: For any organization deploying an AI agent that reads external content, emails, webpages, uploaded documents, connected databases, or tools through a protocol like MCP, this review documents that the realistic risk is not hypothetical, it cites a Copilot vulnerability rated 9.6 out of 10 in severity and a case where a poisoned PDF triggered real damage to physical industrial equipment through a connected AI system, alongside a retrieval augmented system where just five poisoned documents in a knowledge base achieved a 90 percent manipulation success rate. The direct operational implication is that any AI agent with tool access or document retrieval capability should be treated as running in an environment with a wide, difficult to fully close attack surface, meriting layered defenses like the PALADIN framework's input isolation, sandboxing, and anomaly detection working together, mapped against OWASP's LLM security guidance, rather than a single vendor provided safety filter. Because the authors themselves argue complete architectural protection is not currently achievable, procurement and security teams should budget for ongoing monitoring and incident response specifically for prompt injection, not treat it as a one time configuration task, for any AI system connected to untrusted external content today.
papers.explain_practitioner: This review synthesizes 45 sources plus documented security incidents from 2023 to 2025 into a taxonomy covering direct jailbreaking through role play and encoding tricks, indirect injection through poisoned external content like webpages and emails, tool poisoning through malicious descriptions embedded in Model Context Protocol servers including delayed activation rug pull attacks, and RAG poisoning, where the authors report five adversarially crafted documents seeded into a retrieval corpus achieved a 90 percent attack success rate. Documented real world incidents cited include a GitHub Copilot vulnerability, CVE-2025-53773, rated 9.6 out of 10 in severity for enabling remote code execution, and a supply chain style attack the authors call CamoLeak that exfiltrated private repository secrets by bypassing content security policy protections. The authors propose PALADIN, a five layer defense in depth framework spanning input isolation, sandboxed execution, prompt hardening, behavioral anomaly detection, and RAG specific integrity checks, mapped explicitly to the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025. Their stated limitation is architectural, they argue that because large language models process trusted instructions and untrusted data through the same text channel with no hard syntactic boundary, a purely semantic defense can in principle always be bypassed through further social engineering of the prompt.

papers.note: Claims an 85 percent reduction in harmful output with low latency, which is the sort of figure an audit should test rather than accept.
papers.title: Disentangling Adversarial Prompts: A Semantic-Graph Defense for Robust LLM Security
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models can be tricked by prompts that hide harmful intent in unclear wording. This paper introduces a defense called Adversarial Prompt Disentanglement. It tries to separate the malicious parts of a prompt from the safe parts before the model reads it. It combines statistical separation, graph analysis of meaning, and a small classifier trained on toxic and jailbreaking prompts. In tests with adversarial prompts, harmful outputs fell by more than 85 percent, normal performance changed very little, and the method was fast enough for real time use. This matters because safer prompts could make LLMs more trustworthy in security critical settings. The reported figure should be independently audited.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper describes a defense that sits before an LLM and tries to catch jailbreaks and prompt injection before the model responds. The authors claim it can reduce harmful outputs by more than 85 percent, keep normal performance nearly unchanged, and run fast enough for real time use. That informs decisions about deploying LLMs in security critical or customer facing products, choosing vendors, and setting risk controls. It suggests a possible layer for safer AI operations. However, the editor warns that the 85 percent figure should be independently audited, so treat it as a promising claim to test in a pilot, not a guaranteed result.
papers.explain_practitioner: The paper presents Adversarial Prompt Disentanglement, a preprocessing defense for large language models. It has three parts. A mutual information method splits a prompt into adversarial and benign components and aims for statistical independence. A graph based intent classifier uses spectral analysis to find malicious semantic patterns. A lightweight transformer classifier, trained on real world toxic and jailbreaking prompt datasets, detects adversarial intent efficiently. The authors evaluate on diverse adversarial prompt datasets. They report more than 85 percent less harmful output, negligible impact on normal model performance, and computational efficiency suitable for real time deployment. The editor notes this 85 percent claim should be audited.

papers.note: Shows injection combining with cross-site scripting and request forgery, meaning web and AI controls cannot be audited separately.
papers.title: Prompt Injection 2.0: Hybrid AI Threats

papers.note: Finds every one of thirteen frontier models vulnerable and attacks that leave no trace in the user-facing answer, which breaks output-only assurance.
papers.title: How Vulnerable Are AI Agents to Indirect Prompt Injections? Insights from a Large-Scale Public Competition

papers.note: Bypasses all eight tested defences at over 50 percent success, so any vendor injection defence claim needs adaptive testing.
papers.title: Adaptive Attacks Break Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks on LLM Agents
papers.explain_beginner: When a company claims its AI assistant is protected against a specific kind of manipulation, that claim is usually tested by throwing a known, fixed set of attacks at the defense and seeing if it holds up. This paper asks a more adversarial question, what happens if the attacker knows exactly how the defense works and specifically designs their attack to get around that particular defense, rather than reusing an old, generic attack? Zhan and coauthors focused on indirect prompt injection, where an AI assistant that can browse the web or read documents on a user's behalf gets secretly manipulated by hidden instructions planted in that content rather than by the user themselves. They tested eight published defenses meant to stop this kind of attack and found that once they tailored their attacks specifically to each defense's mechanism, every single one of the eight could be broken more than half the time. The clear takeaway is that testing a defense only against old, generic attacks tells you very little about whether it will hold up against someone who actually studies how it works, which is exactly what a real attacker would do.
papers.explain_business: Any vendor or internal team claiming their AI agent is protected against indirect prompt injection, meaning it cannot be secretly manipulated by content it reads from the web or from documents, should be able to demonstrate that the defense survives adaptive testing, an attacker who specifically studies and targets that defense's mechanism, and not just testing against a generic, publicly known attack, because this paper shows all eight defenses examined, spanning multiple different defensive strategies, failed against attacks tailored to them specifically. The direct procurement implication is that a vendor's claim of passing a standard prompt injection benchmark or red team test is not sufficient assurance on its own, since the tested defenses here had also passed their original non-adaptive evaluations before failing adaptive ones. Organizations deploying AI agents with tool or browsing access to untrusted content today should assume current defenses provide partial risk reduction at best against a motivated attacker, and should pair any input level or model level defense with monitoring and limits on what actions the agent can actually take.
papers.explain_practitioner: The study evaluates eight published defenses against indirect prompt injection attacks on LLM agents, spanning detection based approaches such as fine tuned classifiers that flag injected instructions, input level defenses such as delimiting or paraphrasing untrusted content before it reaches the model, and model level defenses such as adversarially fine tuning the underlying LLM or sandwich style prompting that wraps untrusted content with reinforcing instructions. Rather than reusing the static attacks each defense was originally validated against, the authors construct adaptive attacks tailored to each defense's specific mechanism, and report that every one of the eight tested defenses can be bypassed with an attack success rate above 50 percent once the attack is adapted, including defenses like adversarial fine tuning and sandwich prevention that had shown stronger resistance to non-adaptive attacks. The authors' explicit conclusion is methodological, published robustness claims for prompt injection defenses are unreliable when validated only against static or non-adaptive attacks, and adaptive evaluation should be the standard bar going forward, a limitation that applies to essentially all prior defense papers in this space, including some of their own baselines' original evaluations.

papers.note: Classifies attacks by manipulation level and intent, which gives an audit a structure for recording findings consistently.
papers.title: A Systematic Review of Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: Trends, Taxonomy, Evaluation, Defenses, and Opportunities

papers.note: Reports attack success falling from 73 percent to under 9 percent with layered defences, which is a useful benchmark for control effectiveness.
papers.title: Securing AI Agents Against Prompt Injection Attacks

papers.note: Makes the case for system-level rather than model-level controls, which is where an audit should look for enforceable policy.
papers.title: Architecting Secure AI Agents: Perspectives on System-Level Defenses Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
papers.explain_beginner: This paper argues that AI helpers that act on your behalf can be tricked by harmful instructions hidden in untrusted content they read. Instead of relying only on the AI model to resist tricks, the authors say defenses should be built into the whole system around it. They recommend updating plans and security rules as situations change, limiting what the AI can see and decide, and involving people when choices are unclear. They also warn current tests can make systems look safer than they are. This matters because the surrounding design is where enforceable protections can live.
papers.explain_business: For executives, this paper says AI agents that read outside data can be manipulated into unsafe actions, so relying only on the model's judgment is not enough. The authors recommend building controls into the surrounding system: update plans and policies as conditions change, restrict what the model can see and decide, and include human involvement for ambiguous cases. They also caution that current benchmarks may overstate safety and usefulness. In practice, this informs where to invest and audit: guardrails across the whole system, checks based on rules and models, and clear ways for people to be involved, rather than treating model reliability alone as sufficient.
papers.explain_practitioner: This position paper proposes systemwide defenses for AI agents that can be manipulated when untrusted content contains hidden instructions and triggers harmful actions. The authors argue dynamic tasks and realistic settings often require replanning and updated security policies. They say learned models may still handle decisions that depend on context, but only inside designs that tightly limit what those models can see and determine. For unclear cases, tailoring and human involvement should be central design choices. They critique benchmarks falsely suggesting usefulness and safety and argue systemwide defenses structure agent behavior, combine checks based on rules and models, and guide work on model robustness and how people should be involved.

papers.note: Argues data-instruction separation cannot work in principle, which an audit should weigh before accepting it as a sufficient control.
papers.title: AI Agents May Always Fall for Prompt Injections

papers.note: Demonstrates the security tooling itself being hijacked, a reminder that audit tooling is part of the attack surface.
papers.title: Cybersecurity AI: Hacking the AI Hackers via Prompt Injection
papers.explain_beginner: This paper shows that AI tools built to improve cybersecurity can themselves be tricked. The trick is called prompt injection, which is similar to a known web problem called cross-site scripting. Hidden text inside content the AI trusts gets treated as instructions, so the AI does something its creators did not intend. The authors tested this against a real cybersecurity AI framework and its command line tool. They showed attackers could take control of the AI's actions and possibly gain access to systems. The paper also describes layered defenses, and concludes this is a widespread problem needing dedicated fixes.
papers.explain_business: This research shows that AI security tools can be turned against the organizations using them. Attackers can hide instructions in content the AI trusts, causing the tool to act in unintended ways and potentially exposing systems. The authors proved this against a real cybersecurity AI framework and its command line tool, then proposed layered defenses. For executives, the practical takeaway is that AI audit and security tooling is part of the attack surface, not just a safeguard. Decisions about adopting such tools should include assessing prompt injection risk and requiring layered mitigations before deployment.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors demonstrate prompt injection against AI-powered cybersecurity tools, specifically the Cybersecurity AI framework and its CLI. Malicious text embedded in responses from adversarial web servers is interpreted as instructions, hijacking the execution flow of AI agents that find and exploit vulnerabilities, potentially giving attackers system access. They provide proof-of-concept exploits and then describe mitigations implemented as a multi-layered defense. The key result is that prompt injection is a recurring, systemic issue in LLM-based architectures, comparable to cross-site scripting in web applications, and will require dedicated security work to address.

papers.note: Extends the NIST adversarial machine learning taxonomy across 88 studies and catalogues defence effectiveness by model.
papers.title: A Systematic Literature Review on LLM Defenses Against Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking: Expanding NIST Taxonomy
papers.explain_beginner: Large language models can be manipulated with cleverly worded text that makes them ignore their instructions, called prompt injection, or that talks them into producing content they are supposed to refuse, called jailbreaking. Dozens of research teams have proposed ways to defend against both, but the results are scattered across separate papers using different models and different tests, so it is hard to know which defenses actually work. This review reads through 88 of those studies and organizes them using a taxonomy that the US government's NIST agency built for adversarial machine learning, adding new categories NIST had not covered, such as defenses that rewrite the wording of a prompt at the character or token level before the model sees it, and defenses that ask the model to check its own answer. The review finds a few defenses with strong reported numbers. What it does not settle is whether those numbers hold up outside the lab, since the underlying studies rarely test on live production traffic or report what a defense costs in accuracy elsewhere.
papers.explain_business: For any team running a customer facing chatbot, an internal copilot, or an agent that reads untrusted text such as emails or web pages, this review is a usable shortlist of which defenses have real reported numbers behind them rather than marketing claims, including specific fine tuning and dual model architectures that cut attack success sharply in published tests. That said, the review itself warns that these results come from research benchmarks, not live traffic, and rarely say what accuracy or user experience is given up to get them, so a defense that looks strong in a paper still needs to be piloted against an organization's own inputs before being trusted in production. This matters immediately for anyone deploying an LLM that processes content from outside parties, since prompt injection is already an active attack class, not a theoretical future one, and the choice of defense affects both security exposure and ongoing model performance.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors systematically reviewed 88 studies on prompt injection and jailbreak defenses for large language models and extended NIST's adversarial machine learning taxonomy with additional categories, including character, token, and sentence level input perturbation, self reflection checks, decoding steering, defensive pruning, and expanded input and output filtering. Where studies reported numbers, results include Jatmo style fine tuning cutting prompt injection success from as high as 87 percent down to nearly zero while keeping over 98 percent of task performance, and a dual LLM architecture called CaMeL driving attack success to zero against indirect injection on several commercial models. The review's own stated limitation is that these numbers are not comparable across studies, because papers use different datasets, model versions, and settings such as temperature, many do not report the accuracy cost of their defense, and no study in the set tested a defense that combines every strategy the taxonomy now lists.

papers.note: Classifier-based detection with explanation of features, relevant where an audit needs evidence that a filter can be reviewed.
papers.title: Towards Secure AI: Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks with Explainability
papers.journal: 2025 2nd International Conference on Trends in Engineering Systems and Technologies (ICTEST)

papers.note: Proposes adversarial training plus input sanitisation, one of the mitigation patterns an audit would expect to see documented.
papers.title: Advances in AI-Driven Cybersecurity: Tackling Prompt Injection Attacks through Adversarial Learning
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at a new kind of online threat. Chatbots like ChatGPT follow instructions, and attackers can sneak in harmful instructions to make the chatbot say or do things it should not. The researchers studied how these tricks work and then built a defense. Their defense teaches the model to recognize sneaky prompts and also cleans up the text before it reaches the model. When tested, the chatbot resisted these attacks much better, while still working normally. This matters because more businesses and people rely on chatbots, so keeping them safe from manipulation is important.
papers.explain_business: Companies deploying chatbots and LLM tools face a real risk: attackers can manipulate these systems to leak data or produce harmful outputs. This paper shows a practical defense, combining adversarial training with input sanitization, that reduces that risk without noticeably slowing the model or hurting its usefulness. For executives, this supports investing in AI-specific security measures and treating prompt injection as a deployment concern, not an afterthought. It also informs decisions about vendor requirements, audit documentation, and security protocols that adapt as generative models change, helping protect brand trust and customer data.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors analyze prompt injection attacks against LLMs, covering how adversarial prompts bypass content filters, hijack model behavior, and extract sensitive data. They propose a defense framework combining adversarial training with input sanitization to detect and neutralize harmful prompts. Evaluation uses leading LLM platforms, benchmark datasets, and real-world scenarios. Results indicate improved resistance to both direct and indirect prompt injection, with minimal impact on model performance and responsiveness. The work argues for embedding adversarial robustness into the LLM deployment lifecycle and for AI-native security protocols that evolve with generative models.

papers.note: Codes 81 studies against MITRE ATLAS and shows research clusters at the prompt interface, leaving tool and memory boundaries uncovered.
papers.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-Integrated Systems
papers.explain_beginner: This paper looks at how attackers can trick AI systems that use large language models. The problem is that these models cannot tell the difference between real instructions and sneaky text hidden in content they read. The authors reviewed 81 studies and sorted them using a standard security framework. They found that most research focuses on the first point of contact, the prompt, and on two common attack goals. Other parts of real AI systems, like tools and memory, get far less attention. This matters because real systems have many parts, so gaps in research leave real gaps in protection.
papers.explain_business: This review shows that current security research on AI prompt injection is heavily focused on one part of the system, the prompt, while other components like tools and memory are largely ignored. For executives, this means that published defences and threat models may not cover the full attack surface of production AI systems. The decision this informs is where to direct security investment and internal testing. Relying only on prompt-level protections is likely insufficient. Organisations deploying tool-augmented or memory-enabled AI should commission their own assessments of those less-studied boundaries and treat prompt injection as a system-level risk, not just a model-level flaw.
papers.explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a PRISMA systematic review, searching IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and ScienceDirect for peer-reviewed work from 2015 to October 2025. They included 89 publications and analysed 81. Each paper was coded against MITRE ATLAS version 5.4.0 along three axes: trust boundary, attacker objective, and research orientation. Attacker objectives were mapped to seventeen operational patterns. Results show a strong concentration on the prompt interface and on Instruction Hijack and Policy Bypass objectives. Tool and memory boundaries lack both attack characterisation and defence proposals. The authors attribute this to incentives favouring reproducible prompt-level experiments over complex architectural assessments.
